hero.headline: Solar panel complaints mount on Treasure Coast as attorney general investigates companies
hero.body:
Homeowners across the Treasure Coast are coming forward with complaints about solar panel companies, prompting a division of the Florida attorney general's office to take notice. Seniors vs. Crime, a division of the attorney general's office, reached out after an investigation uncovered court records, lawsuits, and a troubling pattern of elderly homeowners who say they were taken advantage of. At least six families have contacted reporters about different companies, but all describe a similar door-to-door sales pitch.

Mike Schopp is now locked into a $60,000 loan for the next 25 years, paying nearly double what he used to. Jane Bibee says her $40,000 solar loan has made it nearly impossible to sell her home. Paula Wass and David McCauley say they are still paying off $39,000 in panels that they say never lowered their nearly $300-a-month FPL bills. McCauley said the whole thing stopped working in November 2024.

Data obtained from the Florida attorney general shows nearly 750 consumer complaints have been filed in Florida against the three solar companies examined in the investigation. Records also show the attorney general has opened formal investigations into two of those companies, and active litigation has been filed against the third. Marty Jacobsen, a deputy director with Seniors vs. Crime, said his office reached out after watching the first report.

In a claim Wass and McCauley filed to seek damages from their solar company, they described a non-functional solar system. An engineering report commissioned by their insurance company found the cause of a leak in their roof was consistent with moisture intrusion at the solar panel brackets. The inspector noted it was not clear if the brackets used to install the solar panels were even an approved system. Seniors vs. Crime has helped multiple homeowners cancel contracts and recover money through mediation and negotiation at no cost. The attorney general's office and Seniors vs. Crime are encouraging anyone in a similar situation to file a complaint.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office increases enforcement after 5 traffic deaths in 4 days
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is increasing traffic enforcement on major roadways after five people died in crashes over four days, including a double fata.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is increasing traffic enforcement on major corridors throughout Martin County following a double fatal crash Monday on Florida's Turnpike near Palm City at Mile Marker 132. The crash marks the fifth traffic fatality in four days in the county. According to investigators, a Tesla traveling south contacted another vehicle, then veered through an opening in the median into the northbound lane where it hit a semi-truck. Three people were inside the Tesla. Two were killed and one was injured and taken to the hospital. Traffic was backed up for hours with lanes shut down in every direction. Richard Cassoon, who works at Stryker Electric just off the Turnpike, said he heard a loud boom and saw vehicles swerving and coming to a complete halt. Northbound and southbound lanes on the Turnpike were shut down for hours while the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol investigated.

Captain Joseph Collazo with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said the recent crashes are top of mind for deputies and the agency is constantly evaluating everything and shifting resources to address problems. With Fourth of July travel ramping up this week, Collazo said deputies will increase enforcement on major corridors throughout Martin County. Collazo asked travelers to slow down and be patient, saying it is not worth losing lives.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County planners recommend approval of Project Tango AI data center
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County planning staff have recommended that county commissioners approve the controversial Project Tango AI data center, despite months of pushback from residents in the western communities.
cards.body:
The proposed data center site sits approximately 1,100 feet from the Arden community and the recently opened Saddleview Elementary School in the western communities of Palm Beach County. As part of the recommendation for approval, county staff are requiring the applicant to make several changes to the plan, including limiting the use of potable water, deeper safeguards for the types and exact placement of the lithium iron batteries, updated sound studies from the Loxahatchee National Wildlife Refuge, and limiting daily water use to 100,000 gallons per day.

Palm Beach County Mayor and Commissioner Sara Baxter, who represents the area where the center would be built, said the staff recommendation simply means the project has met certain legal criteria required by the county. Baxter, who has publicly voiced her opposition to the project and must therefore recuse herself from the vote, said she plans to ask fellow commissioners to do a moratorium on any future data centers until the county gets a grip on what regulations should look like around data centers. Baxter confirmed that if a moratorium is approved, Project Tango would not fall under it.

The next step is a planning and zoning meeting on Thursday, July 2, which is expected to draw hundreds of protesters opposed to the project. Meanwhile, a new law dealing with large-scale data centers is set to take effect Wednesday, July 1. CS/CS/SB 484 sets new utility rules for large load customers, including tariff requirements, and directs a state review of data-center impacts.

cards.headline: 140 new Florida laws take effect today including restaurant fee transparency and local government restrictions
cards.teaser: About 140 new laws take effect Wednesday as Florida begins its new fiscal year, with changes affecting restaurants, local governments, data centers, and more.
cards.body:
About 140 measures take effect Wednesday, July 1, as Florida begins its new fiscal year. The changes span the state budget, data centers, restaurant fees, pet sales, school requirements, local government power and airport names. The largest item taking effect Wednesday is the new state budget. Ron DeSantis signed the Fiscal Year 2026-27 spending plan Monday, totaling about $117.6 billion after nearly $810 million in line-item vetoes.

One of the higher-profile new laws is CS/CS/SB 484, dealing with large-scale data centers. The law sets new utility rules for "large load" customers, including tariff requirements, and directs a state review of data-center impacts. Restaurants face new transparency rules under SB 606, a 2025 law with a delayed July 1, 2026, provision. Restaurants that charge mandatory "operations charges" such as automatic service charges, delivery fees or credit-card surcharges must disclose them on menus, contracts and online ordering platforms and list them separately on receipts. Local governments will see new restrictions on what they can regulate. CS/CS/CS/SB 290 bars counties from banning or restricting certain gasoline-powered farm and landscape equipment, including gas-powered leaf blowers. CS/HB 1217 blocks local governments and other public entities from adopting certain "net zero" or greenhouse-gas-related policies. CS/CS/HB 919 puts the state in control of naming major commercial service airports and points to renaming Palm Beach International Airport as President Donald J. Trump International Airport, subject to federal approval and required agreements.

A Tesla traveling south on Florida's Turnpike near Mile Marker 132 just outside of Palm City made contact with another vehicle Monday afternoon, then veered through an opening in the median into the northbound lane where it struck a semi-truck. Both northbound and southbound lanes on the Turnpike were shut down for hours while the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol investigated.

Captain Joseph Collazo with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said the recent crashes are top of mind for deputies. "We're constantly evaluating everything and shifting resources to try to address problems," Collazo said. With Fourth of July travel ramping up this week, Collazo said the Sheriff's Office will increase enforcement on major corridors throughout Martin County. Collazo urged travelers to do their part to stay safe. "We just ask everyone to slow down and be patient," he said. "We're all trying to get to somewhere, and it's not worth losing our lives over."

cards.headline: Vero Beach nonprofit seeks box truck for Venezuela earthquake relief delivery
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and urgently needs a box truck to transport them to Miami.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network is working with Global Empowerment Mission in Miami to deliver crucial supplies to Venezuela, which is recovering from a 7.5-magnitude earthquake. Lourana Navarro, founder of Latinas Nexus Network, said the organization has been collecting donations since Friday afternoon. The boxes are packed with everything from diapers to medical supplies. The volume of donations is more than the organization can transport on its own.

The organization is now urgently calling on the community to donate the use of a box truck to move the supplies south. Juliana Marino, co-founder of Latinas Nexus Network, said they thought they were just going to put everything in their cars and drive to Miami, but there is no more room. The organization needs a box truck 12 to 16 feet long.

Organizers say they need a box truck no later than Thursday to load it up and deliver the supplies to Global Empowerment Mission in Miami on Friday. Anyone who can help is asked to contact Navarro at 954-205-0700 or Marino at 772-913-0805.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County planning staff recommend approval of controversial AI data center despite western communities pushback
cards.body:
Palm Beach County planning staff have recommended that county commissioners approve the controversial Project Tango AI data center, despite months of opposition from residents in the western communities. The recommendation does not reflect a staff opinion on the merits of the project. County Mayor and Commissioner Sara Baxter, who represents the area where the center would be built, clarified that the staff recommendation simply indicates the project meets certain legal criteria required by county code. "It's not opinion-based. We have certain criteria within the county that has to be met, and all that is saying is that this project meets those certain criteria," Baxter said.

The proposed data center site sits approximately 1,100 feet from the Arden community and the recently opened Saddleview Elementary School. To reduce potential impacts on nearby residents, county staff are requiring the applicant to make several modifications to the plan. These required changes include limiting the use of potable water, implementing deeper safeguards for the types and exact placement of lithium iron batteries, conducting updated sound studies from the Loxahatchee National Wildlife Refuge, and restricting daily water use to 100,000 gallons per day. Despite these conditions, residents who oppose the hyperscale AI data center say the changes are insufficient. Resident Rachel Smith expressed skepticism about the modifications, stating "I appreciate that they're trying to fit within the boundaries of what they need to do, but again, I think it's all a farce." Another resident, Ben Brown, questioned why a heavy industrial process would be located in an area zoned for light industrial use.

Baxter, who has publicly opposed the project and must recuse herself from the vote, plans to push her fellow commissioners to establish a moratorium on future data centers until the county develops appropriate regulations. "I am going to ask my fellow commissioners to do a moratorium on data, any future data centers, until we get a grip on what these regulations should look like around data centers," Baxter said. She emphasized the importance of setting distances from residents and ensuring proper handling of water and power. However, Baxter confirmed that Project Tango would not fall under any approved moratorium. Some residents remain skeptical about Baxter's commitment. Ben Brown noted that if she succeeds in passing a moratorium, it would demonstrate genuine support for constituents. Smith added that multiple counties in Florida have already passed similar moratoriums.

The next step is a planning and zoning meeting scheduled for Thursday, July 2, which is expected to draw hundreds of protesters opposed to the project. Meanwhile, a new state law addressing large-scale data centers, CS/CS/SB 484, takes effect Wednesday, July 1, establishing new utility rules for "large load" customers and directing a state review of data-center impacts.

cards.headline: Boca Raton businesses continue Venezuela earthquake relief as recovery efforts continue
cards.teaser: Local businesses in Boca Raton are continuing their efforts to support families affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela last week, leaving thousands dead and even more missing.
cards.body:
Franky Jorge, owner of GalaFresh Supermarket West Boca Raton, and Pamela Rodriguez, owner of Doctor Chicha, are leading relief efforts for families affected by earthquakes that struck Venezuela last week. Jorge said he moved quickly after hearing about the earthquakes and is now accepting supplies and monetary donations. "Apart from many of our customers being from Venezuela, all of our friends from Venezuela, being Latino, we really feel this as something that really hit close to home," Jorge said.

Rodriguez said dozens of volunteers sorted through non-perishable foods, baby supplies, clothes and more. The donations will be taken to Global Empowerment Mission in Doral and then shipped to families in Venezuela. Rodriguez said the community's response has been overwhelming and noted that one volunteer was an earthquake survivor herself who spent four days trapped under the rubble before being rescued. As recovery continues, Rodriguez stressed the importance of sustained community support. "The most important thing is to keep donating," she said. Jorge echoed that sentiment, saying "today it's Venezuela; tomorrow it can be another place and we just want to make sure we're there to assist no matter where it is."

cards.headline: Jupiter family spends over $1,000 to fix passport errors after using expedited service
cards.teaser: Dr. Thomas McCain and his family discovered five errors in their new passports from the State Department and had to pay more than $1,000 to get them corrected in time for international travel.
cards.body:
A Jupiter family is speaking out after receiving passports with multiple errors and spending more than $1,000 to get them corrected before an international trip. Dr. Thomas McCain contacted WPTV after using the expedited passport system through a local U.S. State Department office. McCain said his passport contained one error, his three children each had the same clerical error, and the middle name of his middle son was also incorrect, totaling five errors across the family's passports. The errors were discovered a month ago and led to hours of phone calls, dead ends and multiple trips to the Palm Beach Gardens post office.

McCain had hoped to travel to England with his family but instead had to travel to Miami to get the passports corrected. "My heart goes out to anybody who is not in a financial position to deal with such or able to take off from work," McCain said. After WPTV contacted the State Department, officials acknowledged the agency has been undergoing large layoffs and reorganization. A State Department spokesperson said the department is committed to providing the best possible service for passport customers while maintaining quality assurance measures throughout the process. If a Department error is identified, the State Department will correct it at no charge within one year.

hero.headline: Solar panel complaints mount on Treasure Coast as attorney general investigates companies
hero.teaser: Seniors vs. Crime, a division of the Florida attorney general's office, reached out after investigations uncovered court records, lawsuits, and a pattern of elderly homeowners who say they were taken advantage of by solar panel companies.
hero.body:
At least six Treasure Coast families have contacted WPTV about solar panel companies after experiencing similar aggressive sales tactics. Jane Bibee says her $40,000 solar loan has made it nearly impossible to sell her home. Mike Schopp is locked into a $60,000 loan for 25 years and now pays nearly double his previous electric bills. Paula Wass and David McCauley report that their $39,000 solar system never reduced their approximately $300 monthly FPL bills, and the system stopped working entirely in November 2024. All these homeowners describe comparable door-to-door pitches emphasizing rising utility rates and promised savings that did not materialize.

The scope of the problem extends well beyond these individual cases. Data obtained from the Florida attorney general shows nearly 750 consumer complaints have been filed against three solar companies examined in this investigation. The attorney general's office has opened formal investigations into two of these companies, with active litigation filed against the third. Seniors vs. Crime, a division of the attorney general's office, became involved after WPTV's initial reporting revealed court records and lawsuits documenting a troubling pattern affecting elderly homeowners who claim they were deceived.

Installation quality and long-term support present additional concerns for affected homeowners. When Wass and McCauley filed a claim seeking damages, they reported their solar system as non-functional. Shortly after installation, they discovered a roof leak. An engineering report commissioned by their insurance company determined the leak was caused by moisture intrusion at the solar panel brackets, and the inspector could not verify the brackets met approved installation standards. Marty Jacobsen, a deputy director with Seniors vs. Crime, explained the broader issue: "Oftentimes, these rogue products are obsolete. They'll go on your roof, they can't connect to the grid, but there's a 25-year warranty with a company that doesn't exist anymore, so you can't get service." Justin Hoysradt, president of Vinyasan Corporation and co-founder of Fix My Solar, noted that poor roof sealing and damaged roofs requiring replacement are common problems he encounters regularly.

Relief options are available for struggling homeowners. Seniors vs. Crime has helped multiple homeowners cancel contracts and recover money through mediation and negotiation at no cost. Attorneys have successfully recovered funds for some homeowners through class-action lawsuits, and Florida's Construction Recovery Fund, financed by permit fees, can compensate consumers who suffer losses due to contractor misconduct. The attorney general's office and Seniors vs. Crime encourage anyone experiencing similar problems to file a complaint with the attorney general's office.

cards.headline: Digital sign in Jupiter Farms warns e-bike riders of fines
cards.teaser: A new Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office digital warning sign on Jupiter Farms Road tells riders that electric motor bikes with no pedals are not legal on streets and sidewalks and operators will be fined.
cards.body:
A new digital warning sign on Jupiter Farms Road is prompting conversations about e-bike safety in the community. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office sign warns that "Electric motor bikes with no pedals, not legal on streets and sidewalks. Operators will be fined." Resident Matthew O'Connor said groups of kids perform wheelies down the middle of the road, sometimes eight riders deep. Fellow resident Debbie Cooper suggested a different approach, proposing that PBSO organize a discussion with the kids and parents at the community center. When contacted for more details about the sign, deputies declined to comment further.

The Jupiter Farms situation reflects a broader trend across South Florida, with communities including Jupiter, Palm Beach, Delray Beach and Boca Raton all passing their own e-bike regulations. The debate reached the state level this week when Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have required e-bike riders to slow to 10 mph when approaching pedestrians on sidewalks and walking paths.

cards.headline: Proposed 25-story development near Singer Island sparks environmental debate
cards.teaser: A proposed $14 million mixed-use project along 2525 Lake Drive in Palm Beach County is raising questions about whether the underwater ecosystem at Phil Foster Park could survive the development.
cards.body:
A New York-based developer, The Continuum Company, has proposed Singer Island Gateway, an approximately $14 million mixed-use project along 2525 Lake Drive. The plan includes hundreds of residential units, commercial and public space, and a marina near the base of the bridge, rising 25 stories at the entrance to Singer Island in Palm Beach County. The proposed development is near Phil Foster Park, where an underwater world thrives that draws divers and snorkelers from across the globe to the base of Blue Heron Bridge.

Longtime resident Gary Heiser, who grew up in the area, said the scale and placement of the project are fundamentally incompatible with the location. Heiser worries that construction activity, increased shade from the tower, and the addition of a marina could disrupt the marine life that has made the reef world-renowned. An environmental study published on the developer's website offers a different assessment. A geoscientist concluded the planned development would have no impact on the marine life in the Lake Worth Lagoon, stating the ecosystem will remain unchanged.

Nothing has been approved yet. The developer has been contacted for comment and a response is pending. Residents have also started a petition against the proposal.

Juliana Marino, co-founder of Latinas Nexus Network, said they thought they were just going to put everything in their cars and drive to Miami, but there is no more room. The organization needs a box truck 12 to 16 feet long.

Organizers say they need a box truck no later than Thursday to load it up and deliver the supplies to Global Empowerment Mission in Miami on Friday. Anyone who can help is asked to contact Navarro at 954-205-0700 or Marino at 772-913-0805.

cards.headline: Tri-Rail receives $60 million to avoid July shutdown
cards.teaser: Florida's new $117 billion state budget includes $60 million for Tri-Rail, which had been at risk of shutting down in July without state help.
cards.body:
One of the biggest wins in the new state budget is for Tri-Rail, which had been at risk of shutting down in July without state help. The commuter rail will receive the $60 million it needed to keep operating. Stanley Lucien, who rides the train from Boca Raton to Miami for business, said it is cheaper and saves a lot of money. Florida State Senator Mack Bernard called the funding a lifeline for commuters.

Palm Beach County also secured money for major infrastructure upgrades, including $1.5 million for the new Riviera Beach water treatment plant and $2 million for drainage repairs to Australian Avenue from 45th Street to Palm Beach Lakes, part of a $65 million total project. The state also approved $3 million for traffic safety improvements on Okeechobee Boulevard. Bernard said over $30 million got approved, representing 75 percent of the funding requested in the budget for Palm Beach County.

Nearly $2 billion in spending proposals were struck from the budget by Gov. Ron DeSantis, including several Palm Beach County priorities. These included $2 million in expansions to parts of the county's water treatment plant, $900,000 for road improvements and beautification in South Bay, $125,000 in improvements to the Ocean Inlet beach access, and $200,000 for repairs and operations at Delray Beach's historic American Legion building.

cards.headline: Indian River State College faces new enrollment restrictions under Florida rule
cards.teaser: Florida's undocumented students could soon face a major new barrier to higher education, with new eligibility requirements affecting Indian River State College and Palm Beach State College.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Education approved new eligibility requirements for adult education and state college programs that require students to be U.S. citizens or lawfully present in the country. The change applies to adult general education programs, including GED preparation courses. Under the updated rule, students enrolling in adult education programs must be at least 16 years old, officially withdraw from traditional school enrollment, and be a U.S. citizen or lawfully present in the United States.

In the Palm Beaches and the Treasure Coast, the changes could affect enrollment at Palm Beach State College and Indian River State College, both recognized Hispanic-Serving Institutions with large Hispanic student populations. According to U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard data, Hispanic students account for roughly 50 percent of enrollment at Indian River State College. At Palm Beach State College, Hispanic students make up about 36 percent of the student body, the school's largest demographic group.

The move comes amid a broader statewide debate over undocumented students' access to public education. The Florida Board of Governors, which oversees the State University System, has discussed similar restrictions that could impact schools including Florida Atlantic University, the University of Florida, and Florida State University. No final vote has been taken on university enrollment restrictions.

cards.headline: Boca Raton restaurant continues Venezuela earthquake relief donation drive
cards.teaser: Local businesses in Boca Raton are continuing their efforts to support families affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela last week.
cards.body:
Franky Jorge, owner of GalaFresh Supermarket West Boca Raton, said he moved quickly after hearing about the earthquakes and is now accepting supplies and monetary donations. Pamela Rodriguez, owner of Doctor Chicha, said dozens of volunteers sorted through non-perishable foods, baby supplies, clothes and more. Those donations will be taken to Global Empowerment Mission in Doral and then shipped to families in Venezuela.

Rodriguez said the community's response has been overwhelming. She said one of the volunteers was an earthquake survivor herself. As the road to recovery continues, Rodriguez said it is important the community does not forget or move on too quickly. Jorge echoed that sentiment, saying the most important thing is to keep donating and pay it forward.
